title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if you can partition the array into two subsets such that the sum of the elements in both subsets is equal.
hints: If the total sum is odd, an equal partition is impossible immediately.
This reduces to: can some subset of nums sum to exactly totalSum / 2? That's the 0/1 knapsack subset-sum problem.

title: Unique Paths II
description: You are given an `m x n` integer array `obstacleGrid` where `1` marks an obstacle and `0` marks free space. A robot starts at the top-left corner and can only move down or right, and cannot pass through obstacles. Return the number of unique paths to the bottom-right corner.
hints: Same idea as Unique Paths, but any cell with an obstacle has exactly 0 ways to reach it (blocking anything that would path through it).

title: Maximal Square
description: Given an `m x n` binary matrix filled with `0`s and `1`s, find the largest square containing only `1`s, and return its area.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the side length of the largest all-1s square whose bottom-right corner is at (i, j).
If matrix[i][j] is 1, dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) — the square can only be as big as its tightest neighbor allows.

title: Target Sum
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`. You must place a `+` or `-` sign before each integer, then compute the sum of all these numbers. Return the number of different ways to assign symbols so the sum equals `target`.
hints: Count how many ways a running sum can be reached after considering each number, using a hash map from sum -> number of ways.
For each number, every existing running sum branches into two: one adding the number, one subtracting it.

title: Perfect Squares
description: Given an integer `n`, return the least number of perfect square numbers (like `1, 4, 9, 16, ...`) that sum to `n`.
hints: dp[i] = fewest perfect squares summing to i, with dp[0] = 0.
For each i, try every perfect square j*j <= i and take dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - j*j] + 1).

title: Palindromic Substrings
description: Given a string `s`, return the number of palindromic substrings in it (substrings starting at different indices are counted as different, even if they consist of the same characters).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Every palindrome expands outward from a center — a single character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length).
Try expanding around every possible center and count how many successful expansions you get in total.

title: Coin Change II
description: You are given an integer `amount` and an array of coin denominations `coins`. Return the number of distinct combinations that make up `amount`, assuming an infinite supply of each coin. Return `0` if the amount cannot be made up by any combination.
hints: Process one coin denomination at a time, updating a dp array of size amount+1 in increasing order of amount — this naturally avoids counting the same combination in different orders as distinct.
dp[a] += dp[a - coin] for every amount a >= coin, for the current coin being processed.

title: Number of 1 Bits
description: Given a non-negative integer `n` (interpreted as its 32-bit binary representation), return the number of `1` bits it has (the Hamming weight).
hints: Repeatedly check the lowest bit with n & 1, then shift n right, counting how many times the bit was 1.
A neat trick: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit — counting how many times you can do that also gives the answer.

title: Single Number II
description: Given an integer array `nums` where every element appears exactly three times except for one, which appears exactly once, find and return that single element.
constraints: Every element appears exactly three times except for one.
hints: For each of the 32 bit positions, sum how many numbers have that bit set — if the total isn't a multiple of 3, the single number has that bit set.

title: Sum of Two Integers
description: Given two integers `a` and `b`, return their sum without using the `+` or `-` operators.
hints: XOR gives the sum of two bits ignoring carry; AND (shifted left by 1) gives the carry produced at each position.
Repeat: newA = a XOR b, newCarry = (a AND b) << 1, until there's no carry left.

title: Reverse Bits
description: Given a non-negative integer `n` (interpreted as a 32-bit binary representation, zero-padded on the left), return the integer value obtained by reversing the order of its 32 bits.
hints: Process the 32 bits one at a time from the least significant end of n, building the result by shifting it left and appending each bit.

title: Happy Number
description: Write an algorithm to determine if a number `n` is happy: repeatedly replace the number by the sum of the squares of its digits, until it either equals 1 (happy), or loops endlessly in a cycle that does not include 1 (not happy). Return `true` if `n` is happy.
hints: Keep a set of numbers seen so far in the sequence — if you see a repeat before reaching 1, it will never reach 1.

title: Power of Two
description: Given an integer `n`, return `true` if it is a power of two, and `false` otherwise. An integer `n` is a power of two if there exists an integer `x` such that `n == 2^x`.
hints: A power of two has exactly one bit set in its binary representation.
For a positive n, n & (n - 1) == 0 exactly when n has a single set bit.

title: Greatest Common Divisor of Two Numbers
description: Given two positive integers `a` and `b`, return their greatest common divisor.
hints: The Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a, b) == gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) == a.

title: Count Primes
description: Given an integer `n`, return the number of prime numbers that are strictly less than `n`.
hints: Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark multiples of every prime found, starting from 2, as composite.
You only need to sieve starting multiples from p*p (smaller multiples were already marked by smaller primes).

title: Pow(x, n)
description: Implement `pow(x, n)`, which calculates `x` raised to the power `n` (i.e., `x^n`). `n` may be negative, in which case the result is `1 / x^(-n)`.
hints: Use fast exponentiation: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2 when n is even, halving the exponent at each step instead of multiplying n times.
Handle negative n by computing the positive-exponent result first, then taking the reciprocal.

title: Fizz Buzz
description: Given an integer `n`, return a string array `answer` (1-indexed) where: `answer[i] == "FizzBuzz"` if `i` is divisible by 3 and 5, `answer[i] == "Fizz"` if `i` is divisible by 3, `answer[i] == "Buzz"` if `i` is divisible by 5, and `answer[i] == str(i)` otherwise.
hints: Check divisibility by 15 first (both 3 and 5), since checking 3 and 5 separately in the wrong order would give the wrong string.

title: Subsets II
description: Given an integer array `nums` that may contain duplicates, return all possible distinct subsets (the power set), with no duplicate subsets in the output.
hints: Sort nums first so that duplicate values become adjacent.
While backtracking, at each recursion level skip a value if it's the same as the previous value tried at that same level — that's what prevents duplicate subsets.

title: Permutations II
description: Given a collection of integers `nums` that might contain duplicates, return all possible unique permutations, in any order.
hints: Sort nums first so duplicate values are adjacent, making them easy to detect and skip.
At each recursion level, skip a value if it equals the previous value and that previous value hasn't been used yet in this branch — that avoids generating the same permutation twice.

title: Combination Sum II
description: Given a collection of candidate numbers `candidates` (which may contain duplicates) and a target number `target`, find all unique combinations where the numbers sum to `target`. Each number in `candidates` may only be used once per combination. Each combination should be listed with its values in ascending order.
hints: Sort the candidates first so duplicate values are adjacent and the running sum grows monotonically as you go deeper.
At each recursion level, skip a candidate value if it's the same as the previous one tried at that same level, to avoid duplicate combinations. Each index can only be used once per branch.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
description: Given a 1-indexed array of integers `numbers` that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific `target`. Return the indices of the two numbers, 1-indexed, as `[index1, index2]`, where `index1 < index2`. You must use only constant extra space.
constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: Since the array is already sorted, a brute-force O(n^2) check is wasteful — use two pointers from both ends instead.
If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if too large, move the right pointer left.

title: 4Sum
description: Given an array `nums` of n integers and an integer `target`, return all unique quadruplets `[nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]]` such that they sum to `target`. Each quadruplet should be listed with its values sorted in ascending order.
hints: Sort the array, then fix the first two numbers with nested loops and solve the remaining two-sum with two pointers, just like 3Sum but one level deeper.
Skip over duplicate values at every level to avoid duplicate quadruplets in the output.

title: Sort Array By Parity
description: Given an integer array `nums`, move all the even integers to the front, followed by all the odd integers, and return the resulting array. Any order within the evens or within the odds is acceptable.
hints: Use two pointers from both ends: whenever the left pointer finds an odd number and the right pointer finds an even number, swap them.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
description: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: The largest squares come from whichever end (leftmost negative or rightmost positive) is farthest from zero.
Fill the result array from the back using two pointers starting at both ends of nums, always placing the larger square next.

title: Backspace String Compare
description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, where `#` means a backspace character, return `true` if they are equal after typing both strings into empty text editors (backspace on an empty string does nothing).
constraints: s and t only contain lowercase letters and '#' characters.
hints: Simulate typing with a stack: push a normal character, pop on '#' (if the stack isn't empty).
Build the final string for both s and t this way, then compare them.

title: Boats to Save People
description: Given an array `people` where `people[i]` is the weight of the `i`-th person, and an integer `limit` for the maximum weight per boat, return the minimum number of boats required to carry every person, where each boat carries at most two people whose sum of weights is at most `limit`.
hints: Sort the people by weight, then greedily pair the lightest and heaviest remaining person together.
If the lightest and heaviest can share a boat, send them both; otherwise the heaviest goes alone. Either way, one boat is used per step.

title: Assign Cookies
description: You have `g[i]` as the greed factor of the `i`-th child and `s[j]` as the size of the `j`-th cookie. A child is content if given a cookie of size at least their greed factor. Each child gets at most one cookie. Return the maximum number of content children.
hints: Sort both the greed factors and the cookie sizes.
Greedily try to satisfy the least greedy child first with the smallest cookie that can satisfy them.

title: Candy
description: There are `n` children standing in a line, each with a rating value given in `ratings`. You must give each child at least one candy. Children with a higher rating than an immediate neighbor must get more candies than that neighbor. Return the minimum number of candies needed.
hints: Start everyone with 1 candy, then do a left-to-right pass, giving one more candy than the left neighbor whenever the rating is higher.
Then do a right-to-left pass, doing the same relative to the right neighbor, taking the max with what's already assigned.

title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
description: Given an integer array `nums` of length `n` where each integer is in the range `[1, n]` and each integer appears once or twice, return an array of all the integers that appear twice.
constraints: Each integer appears once or twice.
hints: A hash set of seen numbers gives an easy O(n) space solution: add each number, and if it's already present, it's a duplicate.

title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
description: Given an array `nums` of `n` integers where `nums[i]` is in the range `[1, n]`, return an array of all the integers in the range `[1, n]` that do not appear in `nums`.
hints: Put every number into a hash set, then check which numbers from 1 to n are missing from it.

title: Third Maximum Number
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the third distinct maximum number in this array. If the third maximum does not exist, return the maximum number.
hints: Track the top three distinct values seen so far as you scan the array once.
If fewer than three distinct values exist by the end, fall back to the maximum.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
description: Given a binary array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the maximum number of consecutive `1`'s in the array if you can flip at most `k` `0`'s to `1`'s.
hints: Slide a window that may contain at most k zeros — expand the right edge, and shrink the left edge whenever the window has more than k zeros.

title: Next Permutation
description: Given an array of integers `nums`, rearrange it into the lexicographically next greater permutation. If no such permutation exists (the array is sorted in descending order), rearrange it into the lowest possible order (sorted ascending). Return the resulting array.
hints: Scan from the right to find the first index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1] — everything after i is already the largest possible suffix.
Swap nums[i] with the smallest value to its right that's still larger than it, then reverse everything after position i.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
description: There are spherical balloons represented as `points[i] = [xstart, xend]` on the x-axis. An arrow shot at position `x` bursts every balloon whose `xstart <= x <= xend`. Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons.
hints: Sort the balloons by their end coordinate.
Greedily shoot an arrow at the end of the first unburst balloon, which also bursts every other balloon overlapping that point; move on to the next balloon that isn't covered.

title: Two City Scheduling
description: A company is planning to interview `2n` people. The cost of flying the `i`-th person to city A is `costs[i][0]`, and to city B is `costs[i][1]`. Return the minimum cost to fly every person to a city such that exactly `n` people arrive in each city.
hints: Start by assuming everyone flies to city A, then decide which n people to switch to city B.
Sort people by how much cheaper city B is relative to city A (costs[i][1] - costs[i][0]), and switch the n people where that saving is greatest.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
description: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. On each day you may buy and/or sell the stock, but you can only hold at most one share at a time (you must sell before buying again). Return the maximum profit achievable.
hints: You never need to hold across a losing day — capture every upward price movement as its own trade.
Sum up prices[i] - prices[i-1] whenever it's positive.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
description: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. Find the maximum profit achievable with at most two transactions (you must sell before buying again).
hints: Track four running states: cost of the first buy, profit after the first sell, cost of the second buy (net of first profit), and profit after the second sell.
Update all four in one linear pass, always taking the best value seen so far for each state.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
description: You are given an integer array `prices` and an integer `k`. Find the maximum profit achievable with at most `k` transactions (you must sell before buying again).
hints: Generalize the two-transaction solution: keep an array of k 'buy' states and k 'sell' states, updating each in order every day.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
description: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the stock price on day `i`. Find the maximum profit, where after selling you cannot buy again on the very next day (a one-day cooldown), and you may hold at most one share at a time.
hints: Track three states per day: holding a share, just sold (in cooldown), and free to buy (not in cooldown).
held[i] = max(held[i-1], rest[i-1] - price); sold[i] = held[i-1] + price; rest[i] = max(rest[i-1], sold[i-1]).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
description: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the stock price on day `i`, and an integer `fee` representing a transaction fee charged once per completed trade. Find the maximum profit, holding at most one share at a time.
hints: Track two running states as you scan: the best profit if currently holding a share, and the best profit if not holding.
Charge the fee once, either at buy or at sell time (pick one and be consistent).

title: Compare Version Numbers
description: Given two version numbers `version1` and `version2`, each a string of numbers separated by dots (leading zeros within a section are ignored), compare them. Return `-1` if version1 < version2, `1` if version1 > version2, and `0` if they are equal.
constraints: Every revision consists of digits only.
hints: Split both versions on '.' and compare the integer value of each corresponding revision in order.
If one version has more revisions than the other, treat the missing ones as 0.

title: Word Pattern
description: Given a `pattern` and a string `s`, both split on spaces for `s`, find if `s` follows the same pattern — a bijection where each letter in `pattern` maps to exactly one word in `s`, and vice versa.
constraints: pattern contains only lowercase English letters.
hints: Maintain two hash maps: letter -> word, and word -> letter, to enforce the mapping is one-to-one in both directions.
The number of words in s must also match the number of characters in pattern.

title: Isomorphic Strings
description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, determine if they are isomorphic — every character in `s` can be replaced to get `t`, with all occurrences of a character mapped to the same character, and no two characters mapping to the same character.
hints: This is the same bijection-checking idea as Word Pattern, just at the character level instead of the word level.

title: Repeated Substring Pattern
description: Given a string `s`, return `true` if it can be constructed by taking a substring of it and appending multiple copies of that substring together.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: A neat trick: s repeats itself if and only if s is a substring of (s + s) with the first and last characters removed.

title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
description: Given a string `s` of `(` and `)` parentheses, return the minimum number of parentheses that must be added to make the resulting string valid.
hints: Track a running balance: increment on '(', decrement on ')'. Whenever the balance would go negative, that ')' needs a matching '(' inserted — count it and reset the balance for that spot to 0.
Whatever balance remains positive at the end also needs that many closing parentheses added.

title: Score of Parentheses
description: Given a balanced parentheses string `s`, return its score based on these rules: `()` has score 1, `AB` (A and B balanced pairs in sequence) has score A + B, and `(A)` has score 2 * A.
constraints: s is a balanced parentheses string.
hints: Use a stack of partial scores: push 0 on '(', and on ')' pop the top and push 2*top back (or 1 if the top was 0), then add it to the new top.

title: Valid Parenthesis String
description: Given a string `s` containing only `(`, `)`, and `*` (which can be treated as `(`, `)`, or an empty string), return `true` if `s` can be made valid.
hints: Track the minimum and maximum possible number of open, unmatched '(' as you scan left to right, given every possible interpretation of '*' so far.
The string is valid if the minimum open count can be kept at 0 or above throughout, and the max never goes negative, and the min ends at exactly 0.

title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
description: Given a string `s` of lowercase letters, `(` and `)`, remove the minimum number of parentheses so the resulting string is valid, and return any valid result.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters, '(' and ')'.
hints: Use a stack of indices to track unmatched '(' — when you hit a ')' with nothing to match, mark it for removal immediately.
Whatever '(' indices remain on the stack at the end also need to be removed. Build the final string by skipping every marked index.

title: Run-Length Encoding
description: Given a non-empty string `s` of lowercase letters, compress it using run-length encoding: each maximal run of a repeated character is written as the character followed by the run's length (a run of length 1 is written as just the character, with no `1`). Return the compressed string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Walk through the string counting consecutive runs of the same character, appending '<char><count>' (or just '<char>' when the count is 1) to the result each time the run ends.

title: Valid Palindrome II
description: Given a string `s`, return `true` if it can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use two pointers from both ends; when a mismatch is found, try skipping either the left or the right character and check if what remains is a palindrome.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
description: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) in `s`.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters.
hints: This is the Longest Common Subsequence of s and its reverse.
Alternatively, build dp[i][j] = longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j], expanding from single characters outward.

title: Zigzag Conversion
description: Given a string `s` and an integer `numRows`, write `s` in a zigzag pattern across `numRows` rows (down then diagonally up, repeating), then read the rows left to right to form a new string. Return that string.
hints: Simulate it directly: keep a list of numRows string buffers, walk through s, and append each character to the current row while bouncing the row index between 0 and numRows-1.

title: Count and Say
description: The count-and-say sequence is defined recursively: `countAndSay(1) = "1"`, and `countAndSay(n)` is the run-length-encoded description of `countAndSay(n-1)` (e.g. "1" -> "11" -> "21" -> "1211" -> "111221"). Given `n`, return `countAndSay(n)`.
hints: Build the sequence iteratively from "1", applying run-length description n-1 times.
To describe a string, scan it in runs of identical consecutive digits, appending '<count><digit>' for each run.

title: Shortest Palindrome
description: Given a string `s`, you may add characters in front of it to make it a palindrome. Return the shortest possible palindrome you can find by performing this transformation.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.
hints: Find the longest prefix of s that is itself a palindrome — everything after it, reversed, needs to be prepended.
Build the string s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute its KMP failure function; the value at the last position tells you the length of that longest palindromic prefix.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description: Given a string `digits` containing digits `2-9`, return all possible letter combinations that the number could represent (standard telephone keypad mapping). Return an empty array if `digits` is empty.
constraints: digits[i] is a digit in the range ['2', '9'].
hints: Backtrack one digit at a time, appending each of that digit's possible letters and recursing to the next digit.

title: Restore IP Addresses
description: Given a string `s` containing only digits, return all possible valid IP addresses that can be formed by inserting three dots into `s` (each segment is 0-255 with no leading zeros unless the segment is exactly "0").
hints: Backtrack by trying every valid length (1 to 3 digits) for each of the four segments.
A segment is valid if it has no leading zero (unless it's exactly "0") and its integer value is between 0 and 255.

title: Word Break II
description: Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return all possible sentences formed by adding spaces into `s` such that each resulting word is in `wordDict`. Words in `wordDict` may be reused any number of times.
constraints: All strings consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use memoized backtracking: for each starting index, try every dictionary word that matches the prefix from there, and recursively solve the rest of the string.
Cache the list of sentences achievable from each starting index so overlapping subproblems aren't recomputed.

title: Wildcard Matching
description: Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p` implementing wildcard matching with support for `?` (matches any single character) and `*` (matches any sequence of characters, including the empty sequence), return `true` if `p` matches the entire string `s`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
p contains only lowercase English letters, '?' or '*'.
hints: Build dp[i][j] = whether s[:i] matches p[:j].
A '*' at p[j-1] can match zero characters (dp[i][j-1]) or one more character of s (dp[i-1][j]) — it's true if either is true.

title: Regular Expression Matching
description: Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p` implementing regular expression matching with support for `.` (matches any single character) and `*` (matches zero or more of the preceding element), return `true` if `p` matches the entire string `s`.
constraints: p contains only lowercase letters, '.', and '*'.
Every '*' is preceded by a valid character or '.'.
hints: Build dp[i][j] = whether s[:i] matches p[:j].
A '*' means: either ignore 'char*' entirely (dp[i][j-2]), or, if the preceding pattern character matches s[i-1], also allow consuming one more character of s (dp[i-1][j]).

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description: Given two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of sizes `m` and `n`, return the median of the two sorted arrays combined. The overall run time complexity should be O(log(m+n)).
hints: Binary search on how many elements to take from the smaller array, so that the combined left half and right half are balanced and every left element is <= every right element.
Once partitioned correctly, the median comes directly from the boundary elements — no need to actually merge the arrays.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
description: There is an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order (not necessarily distinct), possibly rotated. Given `nums` after rotation and an integer `target`, return `true` if `target` is in `nums`, or `false` otherwise.
hints: This is Search in Rotated Sorted Array, but duplicates can make it impossible to tell which half is sorted.
When nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], you can't determine the sorted half — just shrink the range by moving both pointers inward by one.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
description: Suppose an array of length `n` sorted in non-decreasing order (possibly with duplicates) is rotated between `1` and `n` times. Given the rotated array `nums`, return the minimum element.
hints: Same binary search idea as Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, but when nums[mid] == nums[hi] you can't tell which side the minimum is on — just shrink hi by one.

title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
description: Given a sorted array `nums` where every element appears exactly twice except for one element which appears exactly once, return the single element. You must write a solution with O(log n) time and O(1) space.
hints: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices; after it, pairs start at odd indices — binary search for where this pattern breaks.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
description: Given an `n x n` matrix where each row and column is sorted in ascending order, and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th smallest element in the matrix.
hints: Binary search on the value itself: for a candidate value x, count how many matrix elements are <= x by walking from the bottom-left corner (an O(n) count exploiting the sorted rows/columns).
The smallest x where that count is >= k is the answer.

title: Find K Closest Elements
description: Given a sorted integer array `arr`, two integers `k` and `x`, return the `k` closest integers to `x` in the array, sorted in ascending order. An integer `a` is closer to `x` than `b` if `|a - x| < |b - x|`, or `|a - x| == |b - x|` and `a < b`.
constraints: arr is sorted in ascending order.
hints: Binary search for the left boundary of a size-k window: compare how close arr[mid] is to x versus arr[mid + k], and shrink toward whichever side is closer.

title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
description: You are given a mountain array `arr` (strictly increasing then strictly decreasing). Return the index of the peak element.
constraints: arr is guaranteed to be a mountain array.
hints: Binary search: if arr[mid] < arr[mid+1], the peak is to the right; otherwise it's at mid or to the left.

title: Divide Two Integers
description: Given two integers `dividend` and `divisor`, divide them without using multiplication, division, or the modulo operator. Truncate the result toward zero. Assume the environment only allows storage of 32-bit signed integers (clamp the result to `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`).
hints: Repeated subtraction is too slow directly — instead, double the divisor (via bit shifts) as many times as possible before subtracting, similar to long division.

title: Search a 2D Matrix II
description: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for a `target` value in an `m x n` integer matrix where each row is sorted in ascending order from left to right, and each column is sorted in ascending order from top to bottom. Return `true` if found.
hints: Start from the top-right corner: if the current value is bigger than target, move left; if smaller, move down. This eliminates one row or column at each step.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th largest element in the array (the `k`-th largest in sorted order, not the `k`-th distinct element).
hints: A min-heap of size k, scanning through nums and popping whenever the heap grows past k, leaves the k-th largest on top at the end.
Quickselect (a partition-based approach like quicksort) solves this in average O(n) time if you want to avoid the heap.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
description: Given an array of `points` where `points[i] = [xi, yi]` represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer `k`, return the `k` closest points to the origin `(0, 0)`, in any order. Distance is the usual Euclidean distance.
hints: You don't need the actual square-root distance — comparing squared distances (x^2 + y^2) gives the same ordering and avoids floating point.
A max-heap of size k (or a full sort) over squared distance gives the k closest points directly.

title: Top K Frequent Words
description: Given an array of strings `words` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent strings. Sort the answer by frequency from highest to lowest; words with the same frequency are sorted lexicographically (alphabetically ascending).
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of unique words].
hints: Count word frequencies with a hash map, then sort the distinct words by (-frequency, word) so higher frequency comes first and ties break alphabetically.

title: Largest Number
description: Given a list of non-negative integers `nums`, arrange them so as to form the largest possible number, and return the result as a string.
hints: This isn't a plain numeric sort — compare two numbers by which concatenation order (a+b vs b+a) produces the larger string.
Sort all numbers (as strings) using that custom comparator, then join them. Watch out for the all-zeros edge case ("000" should become "0").

title: Asteroid Collision
description: Given an array of integers `asteroids` where the absolute value is the asteroid's size and the sign is its direction (positive = right, negative = left), find the state of the asteroids after all collisions. Two asteroids moving in the same direction never collide. Smaller asteroids explode when colliding with larger ones; equal-size asteroids both explode.
hints: Use a stack: a collision only happens when a right-moving asteroid on the stack meets a new left-moving one.
Resolve each collision by comparing sizes, popping the stack whenever the top asteroid loses, and pushing the new asteroid once nothing left can destroy it.

title: Remove K Digits
description: Given a non-negative integer represented as a string `num`, remove `k` digits so that the resulting number is the smallest possible. Return the result as a string with no leading zeros (unless the result is "0").
constraints: num does not have any leading zeros except for the zero itself.
hints: Use a monotonic increasing stack of digits: while the last digit on the stack is bigger than the current one and you still have removals left, pop it.
After the scan, if removals remain, trim from the end. Then strip any leading zeros.

title: Daily Stock Span
description: Given an array `prices` of the daily price of a stock, return an array `span` where `span[i]` is the maximum number of consecutive days (ending with and including day `i`) that the price was less than or equal to `prices[i]`.
hints: Use a monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs — when the current price is >= the top of the stack, absorb its span and pop it.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
description: Given an array of integers `arr`, find the sum of the minimum value of every contiguous subarray. Since the answer can be large, return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: For each element, figure out how many subarrays have it as the minimum, using a monotonic stack to find the nearest smaller element on each side.
That element contributes value * (distance to previous smaller) * (distance to next smaller) to the total sum.

title: Maximal Rectangle
description: Given a `rows x cols` binary matrix filled with `0`s and `1`s, find the largest rectangle containing only `1`s and return its area.
hints: Treat each row as the base of a histogram, where the height of each column is how many consecutive 1's are stacked above it (including the current row).
Run the Largest Rectangle in Histogram algorithm on each row's height array, and track the overall maximum.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given an array `nums` and an integer `k`, there is a sliding window of size `k` moving from the left of the array to the right, one position at a time. Return an array of the maximum value in the window at each position.
hints: Maintain a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order — the front of the deque is always the current window's maximum.
Before adding a new index, pop from the back while its value is smaller than the new one; pop from the front when it falls outside the window.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the minimum window substring of `s` such that every character in `t` (including duplicates) is included in the window. Return an empty string if no such substring exists.
constraints: s and t consist of English letters.
hints: Expand a window over s until it contains every character of t (by count), then shrink from the left as much as possible while still valid, recording the best window found.
Track how many of t's required distinct characters are currently satisfied in the window, to know in O(1) when the window becomes valid.

title: Subarray Product Less Than K
description: Given an array of positive integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of contiguous subarrays where the product of all the elements is strictly less than `k`.
hints: Slide a window, keeping a running product; shrink from the left whenever the product is >= k.
Every time the window is valid, it contributes (window length) new subarrays — all those ending at the current right pointer.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description: There is an `m x n` rectangular island where `heights[r][c]` is the height above sea level. The Pacific Ocean touches the island's left and top edges, and the Atlantic touches the right and bottom edges. Water flows from a cell to an adjacent cell with height less than or equal to it. Return the coordinates `[r, c]` of every cell from which water can flow to both oceans.
hints: Instead of checking every cell against both oceans (slow), flood-fill outward from the ocean edges instead, moving to cells with height >= the current cell (reverse flow).
Run one flood-fill from all Pacific-adjacent cells and one from all Atlantic-adjacent cells; the answer is every cell reached by both.

title: Surrounded Regions
description: Given an `m x n` matrix `board` containing `1` (representing 'O') and `0` (representing 'X'), capture every region of 1's that is completely surrounded by 0's (not connected to the border) by flipping it to 0. Return the resulting board.
hints: Any 1-region touching the border can never be captured — start by marking every 1 reachable from a border cell.
Every 1 left unmarked after that pass is fully surrounded and should be flipped to 0.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
description: There are `n` cities connected by flights `flights[i] = [from, to, price]`. Given `src`, `dst`, and `k`, return the cheapest price to travel from `src` to `dst` with at most `k` stops in between, or `-1` if no such route exists.
hints: This is a Bellman-Ford-style relaxation: run at most k+1 rounds, where each round relaxes every edge once using distances from the previous round (not distances updated within the same round).
Using a snapshot/copy of the distance array each round prevents using more than the allowed number of stops.

title: Minimum Height Trees
description: A tree is an undirected graph with `n` nodes and `n-1` edges, given as `edges`. Choosing any node as the root gives a tree of a certain height; return every node that, chosen as root, gives the minimum possible height (there can be one or two such nodes).
hints: The roots that minimize height are always the 'center' node(s) of the tree.
Repeatedly peel off all current leaves (degree-1 nodes) layer by layer, like an onion, until 1 or 2 nodes remain — those are the centers.

title: Graph Valid Tree
description: Given `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n-1` and a list of undirected `edges`, return `true` if these edges form a valid tree (connected, and with no cycles).
hints: A valid tree on n nodes has exactly n-1 edges and is fully connected — check the edge count first as a cheap early rejection.
Union-Find (or a single DFS/BFS from any node) confirms connectivity and detects cycles: if you ever union two nodes already in the same component, there's a cycle.

title: Find the Town Judge
description: In a town of `n` people labeled `1` to `n`, the town judge trusts nobody, and everybody (except the judge) trusts the judge. Given `trust`, an array of `[a, b]` pairs meaning `a` trusts `b`, return the label of the town judge, or `-1` if there isn't one.
hints: Track a net trust score per person: -1 for every person they trust (outgoing), +1 for every time someone trusts them (incoming).
The judge is the one person with a score of exactly n - 1.

title: All Paths From Source to Target
description: Given a directed acyclic graph of `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n-1`, given as `graph` where `graph[i]` lists the nodes reachable directly from node `i`, return all possible paths from node `0` to node `n-1`.
constraints: graph[i] does not contain duplicate values.
hints: Backtrack from node 0: append the current path whenever you reach node n-1, otherwise recurse into every neighbor.

title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
description: Given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid`, return the length of the shortest clear path (8-directionally connected, only through cells with value 0) from the top-left to the bottom-right corner, or `-1` if no such path exists.
hints: BFS gives the shortest path length in an unweighted graph — here, each cell's 8 neighbors are its graph edges.
Remember to check that both the start and end cells are themselves clear (value 0) before starting.

title: As Far from Land as Possible
description: Given an `n x n` grid containing only `0`s (water) and `1`s (land), find the water cell that maximizes its distance (Manhattan) to the nearest land cell, and return that distance. Return `-1` if no water or no land exists.
hints: Multi-source BFS from every land cell simultaneously finds, for every water cell, its shortest distance to any land in one pass.
The answer is the maximum distance reached during that BFS.

title: 01 Matrix
description: Given an `m x n` binary matrix `mat`, return the distance of the nearest `0` for each cell (distance measured in 4-directional steps).
hints: Multi-source BFS starting from every 0 cell at once finds the nearest-0 distance for every cell in a single pass.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
description: You have a graph of `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n-1`, given a list of undirected `edges`. Return the number of connected components in the graph.
hints: Union-Find each edge, merging the two endpoints' components; the number of distinct root components remaining is the answer.

title: Critical Connections in a Network
description: There are `n` servers labeled `0` to `n-1` connected by `connections`. A critical connection (bridge) is one that, if removed, disconnects part of the network. Return all critical connections, each reported with the smaller-numbered endpoint first.
hints: This is Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm: track each node's discovery time and the lowest discovery time reachable from it (its 'low-link' value).
An edge (u, v) is a bridge exactly when v's low-link value is strictly greater than u's discovery time — meaning v's subtree has no other way back to u or above.

title: Triangle
description: Given a `triangle` array where `triangle[i]` has `i+1` elements, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom, moving from row `i` to either index `j` or `j+1` in row `i+1` at each step.
hints: Work from the bottom row upward: each cell's best path sum is its own value plus the smaller of the two cells below it.
This shrinks the whole triangle down to a single value at the top — the answer.

title: Delete and Earn
description: Given an integer array `nums`, you earn points by picking any `nums[i]`, deleting it and every other element equal to `nums[i] - 1` or `nums[i] + 1`. Return the maximum number of points you can earn.
hints: This reduces to House Robber: sum up all points available for each distinct value, then you can't take two point-totals from adjacent values.
Build an array indexed by value (points[v] = v * count of v in nums), then run House Robber's DP over it.

title: Ones and Zeroes
description: You are given an array of binary strings `strs` and two integers `m` and `n`. Return the size of the largest subset of `strs` such that there are at most `m` `0`'s and `n` `1`'s in total across the subset.
hints: This is a 2D knapsack: dp[i][j] = largest subset size using at most i zeros and j ones.
For each string, count its zeros/ones, then update dp from high (m, n) down to low so each string is only used once.

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
description: Given an `n x n` integer matrix, return the minimum sum of a falling path: starting at any cell in the first row and, at each step, moving to a cell in the next row that is directly below or diagonally adjacent.
hints: Work row by row from the top: each cell's best falling-path sum is its own value plus the smallest of the three reachable cells above it.
The answer is the minimum value in the final (bottom) row after this pass.

title: Count Square Submatrices with All Ones
description: Given an `m x n` binary matrix, return the total number of square submatrices that consist entirely of `1`'s.
hints: The largest all-1s square ending at (i, j) has side length 1 + min(the same value at the cell above, to the left, and diagonally above-left) — same idea as Maximal Square.
Every possible square side length ending at a cell counts as its own valid square, so summing this dp value across the whole grid gives the total count directly.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
description: You are given an array `cost` where `cost[i]` is the cost of stepping on stair `i`. Once you pay the cost, you can climb one or two steps. You start at index 0 or index 1, and the top of the staircase is one step past the last index. Return the minimum cost to reach the top.
hints: dp[i] = minimum cost to reach step i = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]).
The answer is the cheaper of reaching the top from the last step or the second-to-last step.

title: Russian Doll Envelopes
description: You are given a 2D array `envelopes` where `envelopes[i] = [wi, hi]`. One envelope can fit into another if both its width and height are strictly smaller. Return the maximum number of envelopes you can nest inside each other (like Russian dolls).
hints: Sort by width ascending, but for equal widths sort by height descending — that prevents same-width envelopes from being nested into each other.
After sorting, the answer is the Longest Increasing Subsequence of the heights.

title: Burst Balloons
description: You are given `n` balloons in a row, indexed `0` to `n-1`, represented by `nums`. Bursting balloon `i` earns `nums[left] * nums[i] * nums[right]` coins, where `left`/`right` are the current adjacent balloons (treat out-of-bounds as having value 1). Return the maximum coins achievable by bursting all balloons in some order.
hints: Think in reverse: instead of which balloon to burst first, decide which balloon to burst LAST within each subrange.
Pad nums with a 1 on both ends, then let dp[l][r] be the max coins from bursting every balloon strictly between l and r; try every choice of the last balloon burst in that range.
